title: Minimal Runtime KV Relocate/Rebind Primitive
patch_scope_summary: 4 files, 173 raw insertion lines (0 deletions), see patch_scope.json
api_shape: bool llama_kv_cache::relocate_layer(int32_t il, ggml_backend_buffer_type_t new_buft, bool retain_old_backing_for_research = false) -- llama-kv-cache.h/.cpp, plus a thin C-API wrapper llama_kv_cache_relocate_layer(llama_memory_t, int32_t, ggml_backend_dev_t, bool = false) in llama.h/llama-context.cpp.
ownership_model: Every relocation allocates a brand-new, dedicated (ggml_context, ggml_backend_buffer_t) pair appended to llama_kv_cache's existing ctxs_bufs vector -- never a slice of the shared construction-time bulk buffer other layers may still occupy. Old backing is physically freed only when a live scan of `layers` confirms no other layer still references it (true starting from a layer's SECOND relocation onward, never true on its first move away from the shared bulk buffer).
synchronization_contract: relocate_layer may only be called between decode calls, with the backend already synchronized (llama_synchronize()) -- documented in llama-kv-cache.h. This phase found that satisfying this contract is NECESSARY but not SUFFICIENT for safe old-backing release (see release_failure.json).
cpu_to_gpu_result: PASS -- see single_cpu_gpu.json. Pointer changed, destination device correct, poison test confirms live rebind (classification A).
gpu_to_cpu_result: PASS -- see single_gpu_cpu.json. Same, reverse direction.
repeated_same_layer_retained_result: PASS -- see repeated_same_layer_retained.json. With retain_old_backing_for_research=true (old backing intentionally leaked, never a memory optimization), a SECOND relocation of the SAME layer (CPU->GPU->CPU) is functionally correct: ground-truth poison test proves decode consumes the post-relocation-2 backing, not the stale one, even though the probe's own diagnostic tensor-pointer capture misleadingly still reports the relocation-1 identity (a confirmed measurement artifact, not a decode bug).
poison_ground_truth_result: Consistent PASS across every trial this phase (single CPU->GPU, single GPU->CPU, repeated same-layer with retained backing) -- see poison_test.json.
release_enabled_failure: Reproducible crash when the SAME sequence runs with the real default (retain_old_backing_for_research=false, i.e. old backing release attempted): freeing a layer's now-orphaned dedicated backing on its second relocation crashes the NEXT llama_decode() call. Two distinct crash signatures observed across this investigation: SIGSEGV (this session's reproducer, reproducible across repeated trials and a 4-decode settling-window variant) and GGML_ASSERT(buffer != nullptr) at ggml-vulkan.cpp:7815 ggml_vk_tensor_subbuffer (an earlier session, different call pattern). A third, structurally similar call pattern (mode=roundtrip) did NOT crash across 4 repeated runs -- disclosed honestly as non-uniform, call-pattern-dependent manifestation, NOT as evidence that pattern is safe. See release_failure.json.
external_vram_rss_changes: Not independently re-measured in this closing checkpoint beyond what single_cpu_gpu.json/single_gpu_cpu.json/raw_roundtrip_*.json already show (real, small VRAM deltas consistent with allocator overhead) -- superseded in priority by the release-safety finding, which makes further VRAM-release characterization premature until release itself is fixed.

maintenance_assessment: See maintenance.json -- moderate conflict risk (reads llama_kv_cache internals under active upstream development), rebind mechanism plausibly upstreamable, release mechanism is not upstream-ready given the demonstrated crash.
what_is_proven: The Phase 12C hypothesis (a pointer-rebind primitive is sufficient) is CORRECT for the rebind itself -- proven via ground-truth poison testing across every direction and repetition tested, not asserted from code reading.
Live persistent KV tensor binding CAN change safely at runtime, repeatedly, for the SAME layer, PROVIDED the old backing is retained (never freed).
Weight placement is independent of and unaffected by KV relocation.
The primitive is precision-agnostic (Q8_0/Q5_1) and not tied to one model's layer geometry.
The patch is small, additive-only (0 deletions), and reproducibly applies cleanly on a fresh reset of the pinned submodule plus the two prior patches.
what_remains_unknown: The exact internal owner of the stale reference that makes freeing old backing unsafe -- candidates were considered (ggml_backend_sched's prev_*_backend_ids arrays, Vulkan buffer-pool reuse) but none was conclusively confirmed within this phase's scope.

Whether the release crash is Vulkan-backend-specific or would also occur on the CPU backend alone (not tested -- CPU-only builds on this host have no second backend to relocate to/from, see Phase 12C's own equivalent limitation).

Whether a different (non-'always retain') release strategy -- e.g. deferred/batched release, or release only after N settled decodes measured empirically rather than assumed -- could be made safe; the one settling-window variant tested did not help, but the space of possible mitigations was not exhaustively searched.
limitations: This closing checkpoint deliberately skipped the full original Section 7-30 benchmark matrix (context matrix, pressure-regime test, cycle stability, latency breakdown, state save/load, defrag/shift interaction tests, graph-split-count measurement) per explicit instruction, since none of it can change the verdict once release was shown unsafe.

Two crash signatures (SIGSEGV, GGML_ASSERT) were observed for what is believed to be the same underlying issue, across different sessions/call patterns -- not verified to be the identical fault via a debugger, only via consistent circumstances (always the decode immediately following a second same-layer relocation with release enabled).
Vulkan+ASan/UBSan was not attempted (resource risk, same reasoning as Phase 12C).
decision_gate_meaning: Runtime rebind itself is functional: repeated relocation of the same layer works, and decode provably consumes the newly-rebound backing (poison-test ground truth). Old backing cannot currently be safely released -- retaining old buffers avoids the crash but defeats true dynamic-memory reclamation. The primitive is therefore not yet suitable for real tiering.
next_step_recommendation: Investigate and design safe backend-buffer retirement / lifetime ownership for relocated KV backing.
